name: Beck, Katz & Tucker (1998) 'Taking Time Seriously: Time-Series-Cross-Section Analysis with a Binary Dependent Variable' + Carter & Signorino (2010) 'Back to the Future: Modeling Time Dependence in Binary Data' (plus Beck 2010 'Time Is Not a Theoretical Variable' and the Carter-Signorino reply)
type: method family (two peer-reviewed methods papers on discrete-time hazard / duration dependence in binary panel data)
url: BKT 1998: https://doi.org/10.2307/2991857 (AJPS 42(4):1260-1288); author PDF: https://websites.umich.edu/~franzese/BeckKatzTucker.TakingTimeSeriously.AJPS1998.pdf ; working paper 'Beyond Ordinary Logit' (1997): https://authors.library.caltech.edu/80367/ . Carter & Signorino 2010: https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpq013 (Political Analysis 18(3):271-292); https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/back-to-the-future-modeling-time-dependence-in-binary-data/9E4BCC2A63726C4ECD63F236C49AF9FA ; web appendix with R/Stata code: https://static.cambridge.org/content/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:article:S1047198700012456/resource/name/S1047198700012456sup001.pdf
year: 1998 (BKT; working paper 1997); 2010 (Carter & Signorino, online 15 Jun 2010; Beck's comment and the authors' reply appeared in the same 2010 issue)
authors: Nathaniel Beck, Jonathan N. Katz, Richard Tucker (1998); David B. Carter, Curtis S. Signorino (2010)
popularity: Both are standard references in political science. BKT 1998 has several thousand Google Scholar citations and C&S 2010 more than a thousand; exact counts were not retrieved [uncertain]
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed (American Journal of Political Science; Political Analysis)
target_type: Onset (event start). In the canonical application (militarized interstate dispute onset in dyad-years, from Oneal & Russett 1997), the dependent variable is the START of a new dispute. Years of an ongoing dispute after its first year are dropped, so the unit is not 'at risk' of a new onset in those years. This is a hazard (onset) target, not a state target, so it matches our project's target type.
target_definition: y_it = 1 if an event starts for unit i in discrete period t (here year t), else 0. The horizon is one discrete period: H = 1 interval of the grouping (a year in BKT). BKT show that this binary TSCS set-up is identical to grouped (discrete-time) duration data: P(y_it = 1 | no event since last one) is a discrete hazard h(t - t0). With a cloglog link this is exactly a grouped continuous-time Cox/proportional-hazards model. A logit link is a close approximation when events are rare.
spatial_unit: Cross-sectional unit = dyad (country pair) in BKT and in most replications. C&S also replicate country-level and organisation-level data (Crowley & Skocpol 2001 on US civic associations; Palmer, London & Regan 2004). No geographic grid.
at_risk_masking: Yes, in the canonical application: ongoing-event periods are excluded and only onset periods count, so the risk set is units not currently in an event. This is the discrete-time-hazard version of our D-rule 'rows already under alert at t are masked'. BKT discuss that the counter of 'peace years' restarts after each event ends. That makes the risk set and the time-since counter depend on knowing when the previous event ENDED. In our setting the end must be observed by t (D-020 causal 24h cap).
data_sources: BKT: Oneal & Russett (1997) dyad-year data on militarized interstate disputes (Correlates of War MID), politically relevant dyads, roughly 1950-1985 (about 20k dyad-years) [uncertain on exact N/years]. C&S: Monte Carlo simulations plus replications of Oneal & Russett (1997), Palmer, London & Regan (2004), and Crowley & Skocpol (2001).
data_source_variant: Not applicable (no air-alert data). The methods are generic for binary panels where an event can recur within a unit.
preprocessing: Construct a per-unit counter of periods since the last event ('peace years'), which resets after each event. Drop ongoing-event periods after onset. Handle left censoring: the counter at the start of the panel is unknown, because events before the observation window are not seen. BKT note this issue and use the panel start (or an earlier known event) as the origin. Optionally add the number of previous events (a repeated-failure covariate).
known_label_artefacts: Not about alerts. Analogous issues they raise: (1) left-censored duration counters at series start, the analogue of our 2022-03-23 start where the first 'time since last end' is unknown; (2) ties and the coarseness of grouping, since a yearly grid hides within-period timing (our hourly grid hides within-hour timing, and multiple sub-oblast onsets within an hour collapse to one); (3) with time dummies, separation arises at durations where all observations are 0 (or 1). Those rows are dropped by logit software or yield infinite coefficients, the problem C&S highlight; (4) events whose end is ambiguous, which shift the counter. None of these papers has alert-specific artefacts such as 30-min ends, standing alerts or recording gaps.
model_family: Discrete-time hazard via binary GLM (logit, or cloglog for exact grouped proportional hazards). Duration dependence is modelled in three ways. (a) BKT: a full set of time-since-last-event dummies (a non-parametric baseline hazard), or a natural cubic spline of the counter (BKT used 3 knots, the best smoother available in Stata then). (b) C&S: a cubic polynomial t, t^2, t^3 of time since last event. (c) C&S also compare auto-smoothing methods (GAM-type splines) and LOWESS.
features: Core duration features: time since last event (counter t), entered as dummies, a natural cubic spline or a cubic polynomial (t, t^2, t^3). Optional: number of previous events, and interactions of t with covariates (non-proportional hazards; C&S stress this is easy with the polynomial). Substantive covariates in the application are dyad-level (trade dependence, democracy, alliance, contiguity, capability ratio, growth). Spatial or contagion features are not part of the core method. Beck and co-authors treat spatial dependence in separate later work (Beck, Gleditsch & Beardsley 2006) [uncertain on that pointer's exact scope].
external_feature_timing: Not applicable. Covariates are annual and lagged one period in the application, so they are observed before the outcome period.
ablation_design: BKT compare ordinary logit with logit plus duration terms on the same dyad-year sample and test the joint significance of the time dummies or spline terms (a likelihood-ratio / Wald test as a diagnostic for temporal dependence). In the Oneal & Russett reanalysis, the trade coefficient shrinks substantially once duration dependence is controlled [uncertain on exact magnitude]. C&S compare dummies, splines, the cubic polynomial and auto-smoothers on the same simulated and replicated samples.
split_scheme: No out-of-sample or walk-forward evaluation. Both papers estimate in-sample (inference-oriented political science). C&S evaluate methods by Monte Carlo recovery of known hazard shapes.
metrics: In-sample coefficients, standard errors, likelihood-ratio tests, and recovery of the true baseline hazard in simulation (bias/MSE of the fitted hazard curve). C&S compare logit and cloglog fits in the appendix. No Brier, AUC or PR-AUC.
unit_of_metric: Not applicable (no predictive metric). Inference is pooled across units.
baseline_strength: The implicit baseline is ordinary pooled logit that ignores duration dependence. Their main finding is that it gives over-confident standard errors and biased coefficients. No climatology or rolling-rate forecasting baseline.
calibration: Not addressed as forecast calibration. C&S check fit of the baseline hazard shape and note logit vs cloglog differences are small for rare events.
calibration_under_drift: Not addressed. The methods assume a stable baseline hazard in t across the panel, apart from covariates. Calendar-time trends are a separate issue: C&S's appendix tests the polynomial and splines with a time-trended covariate. Beck (2010) argues that duration terms are a stand-in for unmodelled processes. That warns that a fitted hazard shape may not transfer when the process changes, for example after the Sep-2026 yellow/red reform.
uncertainty_of_gain: Standard errors and likelihood-ratio tests only. No forecast skill CI.
regime_coverage: Not applicable to air alerts. Methodologically they assume a stationary duration-dependence shape. Regime shifts would need interactions of t with period indicators (non-proportional hazards in calendar time). C&S say their method makes such interactions straightforward.
leakage_handling: Not a forecasting paper, so leakage is not discussed in ML terms. The construction is causal by design: the counter at period t uses only the timing of past events, so it is a legitimate 'known at t' feature if (i) the end of the previous event is known by t and (ii) no future information sets the counter. Our project-specific traps: (1) 'time since last END' needs the end to be observed by t. Under D-020 an alert still running is either active (masked) or past 24h (standing). The end of a standing alert is not known at t, so the counter must use the causal end (min(observed end, start+24h)) and never the final finished_at. (2) Left censoring at series start and after the 2026-08-30 to 09-01 gap: the counter must be NaN or flagged, not computed as if no alert happened during the gap (D-013). (3) Time dummies or splines fit on the full data (knots chosen from full-data quantiles) are a mild leak. Knots or bins should be chosen on train only, in line with the 'no scalers fit on full data' rule.
test_window_hygiene: Not applicable (in-sample inference). Note: BKT's diagnostic (joint significance of duration terms) can be done on train/validation only, keeping the final test untouched.
headline_results: BKT 1998: binary TSCS data are grouped duration data. Ordinary logit ignoring this assumes temporal independence, which is often violated, and gives over-confident standard errors. Adding time-since-last-event dummies or a natural cubic spline (a discrete-time hazard logit) fixes this and gives a test for duration dependence. In the Oneal & Russett trade-and-peace reanalysis, duration dependence is strong and negative (the hazard of a new dispute falls with peace years). The pacifying effect of trade weakens and loses significance once it is modelled [uncertain on exact numbers]. Carter & Signorino 2010: time dummies cause quasi-complete separation, inefficiency and dropped observations when some durations have no events. Splines need knot choices and are hard to interpret. A cubic polynomial in time since last event (t, t^2, t^3) recovers the common hazard shapes (decreasing, increasing, non-monotone) about as well as splines or auto-smoothers in Monte Carlo, beats time dummies, and makes non-proportional hazards (t x covariate interactions) easy. In the 2010 exchange, Beck argues that 'time is not a theoretical variable': duration terms soak up omitted dynamics and should not be over-interpreted. C&S agree the cubic is an approximation, a special case of cubic splines, not a claim of superiority. These papers report no predictive skill numbers, so there is no comparison against naive forecasting baselines.
code_available: C&S web appendix gives R and Stata code for the cubic polynomial and splines (Cambridge supplementary PDF). BKT's original BTSCS Stata routine (btscs.ado, by Tucker) circulated widely, for example on Statalist. Oneal & Russett replication data are available via the authors and journal archives [uncertain on current hosting].
takeaways_for_project: 1) Theoretical justification for the own-state features: our hourly per-oblast onset task is exactly BKT's binary TSCS = grouped duration data. P(onset in (t, t+1h] | not under alert at t) is a discrete-time hazard, so minutes_since_last_end and minutes_since_last_start are the duration-dependence terms BKT say must be included. Without them a pooled classifier assumes hours are independent, which they are not. 2) The at-risk mask (target rule: drop rows under alert at t) is the risk-set definition of a discrete hazard model, the same as BKT dropping ongoing-dispute years. Cite BKT in the README to explain why masking is principled, not a convenience. 3) Counter reset and causal end: BKT's counter restarts at the event END. Ours must use the causal end under D-020 (an alert stops counting at start+24h if no end is observed by then). Never use the final finished_at. Add a leakage-test case for that. 4) Left censoring: the first alert history of each oblast (2022-03-23) and the 2026-08-30 to 09-01 recording gap (D-013) make the counter unknown. Set it to NaN or flag it, which BKT and the survival literature support. Do not fill it with large values as if there were peace. 5) Functional form: for a GBM, raw minutes_since_* is enough (trees approximate the hazard non-parametrically). For a logistic baseline or interpretable model, use log(1 + minutes) or C&S's cubic polynomial / a natural spline with train-only knots. Avoid one-hot time dummies at fine resolution (separation, C&S). 6) Repeated events: BKT's 'number of prior events' maps to onsets_last_24h / 7d. These capture self-excitation (clustering of waves) that a single time-since counter misses (link to Hawkes-type models). 7) Link: with H = 1h and rare onsets in rear oblasts, logit ~ cloglog. If H becomes configurable and large, cloglog is the exact grouped-hazard link. Optionally note this when H > 1. 8) Non-proportional hazards: C&S recommend t x covariate interactions. The analogue is letting the time-since effect differ by group (frontline vs rear vs Kyiv City) or by hour of day. A GBM gets this for free; a logistic baseline needs explicit interactions. 9) Diagnostic / ablation: reproduce BKT's test as an ablation on the SAME masked train/validation rows: model without vs with time-since features, compared on validation Brier/BSS (never the final test). That gives empirical evidence that duration dependence matters, rather than relying only on feature importance. 10) Beck's 2010 caution: the fitted hazard shape is a reduced-form proxy for unobserved attack dynamics. After the Sep-2026 yellow/red reform the shape may change, so the D-015 transfer section should say a failure of time-since effects to transfer is expected, not a contradiction.
best_practices: Adopt: (a) treat the onset task explicitly as a discrete-time hazard with a proper risk set (mask rows under alert); (b) include time since last event (end and/or start) as a core feature, causally constructed; (c) smooth duration terms: cubic polynomial or natural spline for linear models, raw or log values for trees; choose knots/bins on train only; (d) include a count of recent events for multiple-failure / self-exciting dynamics; (e) test duration dependence by ablation on an identical sample; (f) handle left censoring and data gaps explicitly (NaN or flag); (g) consider cloglog when the horizon is coarse; (h) allow non-proportional effects (interactions with group or calendar). Avoid: (i) ordinary pooled logit/classifier with no temporal terms, treated as if rows were independent; (ii) fine-grained time dummies that cause separation and dropped rows; (iii) counters reset by an end time that is not yet observed (leakage), or that silently run through recording gaps; (iv) interpreting the fitted hazard curve causally ('time is not a theoretical variable'); (v) keeping ongoing-event rows in an onset model, which conflates state persistence with onset and inflates scores; (vi) assuming the duration-dependence shape is stable across regime changes without checking.
